prompt: The speaker's central claim about the sea is that it
passage:
LOW TIDE AT MAREN POINT

The bay goes out at four and leaves behind
a country it has copied from itself:
small rivers running nowhere in the mud,
ridges the colour of a folded sheet.

I walk the flat and read what has been written—
a scribble where a crab went sideways home,
the drag-mark of a bird's indecisive foot,
and everywhere the pocks of buried air.

My grandmother would say the sea forgets,
and pull her collar up, and turn for shore.
I think it is the opposite of that.
The sea remembers every single thing

and puts it down in mud so it will go.
The water climbs at nine and takes it back—
the crab, the bird, the scribble, and my prints,
which were the last thing written, and the least.
choices: carries away more each season than it ever returns
keeps its shape more faithfully than the land it borders
sets down a record of what has passed and then removes it
reveals at low tide the shape it will take at high tide
is indifferent to whatever crosses the flat between tides
correct_answer: sets down a record of what has passed and then removes it
explanation: The third and fourth stanzas run together into a single claim: "The sea remembers every single thing // and puts it down in mud so it will go," and then "The water climbs at nine and takes it back." That is a record made and then unmade, which is what "sets down a record of what has passed and then removes it" describes. "is indifferent to whatever crosses the flat between tides" is the grandmother's view, not the speaker's; the speaker says "I think it is the opposite of that."

prompt: The author's main purpose in the passage is to
passage:
For eleven years I have stood at a desk and taken quarters from children. I want to explain why my library has stopped.

The case for fines is easy to state, and I will not pretend otherwise: a book that is out is a book nobody else can read, and a small penalty is a cheap way to remind a borrower of that. Libraries that dropped their fines were warned that their shelves would empty. It is a serious argument, and for a long time it was mine.

What changed my mind was not a principle but a spreadsheet. Our fines brought in about four thousand dollars a year, of which roughly a third went straight back out in the cost of collecting it — the notices, the postage, the staff hours spent at the desk arguing over a dollar forty. Against that we blocked, on an average day, thirty-one accounts. Blocking an account does not produce a returned book. It produces a family that stops coming.

And the accounts we blocked were not distributed evenly. They belonged, overwhelmingly, to the branches serving the lowest median household incomes. A fine of ten cents a day is a rounding error to one family and a reason to stay home to another, which means that the same rule was doing two entirely different jobs depending on the address of the person it was applied to. Whatever we were charging for, we were not charging everyone.

The prediction about empty shelves can now be tested, because more than four hundred systems have tried it. Our own return rate, eighteen months on, is within one percentage point of what it was — slightly worse, in fact, and I would rather report that than round it away. What did move was traffic: circulation at our two smallest branches is up by a fifth, and eleven hundred lapsed borrowers have come back.

I am not arguing that a library should be indifferent to its books. We still bill for a book that is genuinely lost, and that bill is not small. The difference is that we now charge for the loss of a book rather than for the passage of time, and only the first of those was ever something a borrower chose.
choices: compare the fine policies of several library systems in detail
urge borrowers to return their books before the date they are due
describe the daily work of a librarian at the circulation desk
explain why her library ended a practice she had once defended
propose a new schedule of fees to replace the one she dropped
correct_answer: explain why her library ended a practice she had once defended
explanation: The opening states the task — "I want to explain why my library has stopped" — and the second paragraph concedes that the case for fines "for a long time … was mine." "explain why her library ended a practice she had once defended" covers both halves. "propose a new schedule of fees to replace the one she dropped" is refused by the last paragraph, which keeps only the existing bill for a lost book.
